newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Sackings just one shot in Russia army reform war.
newsitem.headline: Sackings just one shot in Russia army reform war.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin hailed the dismissal of his defence minister on Thursday as a decisive shot in the battle to reform the military, but defence experts questioned whether it was enough to turn the tide.

Yeltsin sacked Defence Minister Igor Rodionov and the chief of the general staff, Viktor Samsonov, at a meeting of the advisory Defence Council. He accused them of doing nothing to start reforms and said: "I have taken a powerful step today."

But after years of unfulfilled Kremlin pledges to shake up the demoralised and underfunded armed forces, many military analysts and critics say an injection of money backed by a firm political will is the only guarantee that reforms will succeed.

"The sacking could be a good thing if Yeltsin takes personal charge of the reforms or sets up a special body to deal with them. A strong political will is needed," said Mikhail Gerasev, a military expert at the independent USA and Canada thinktank.
But he added: "Military reforms are costly. If you want the reforms to succeed, you have to be prepared to spend."
Defence analysts said Rodionov had achieved little in less than a year in office and his position had long been weak, although his dismissal had not been expected at this stage.
They said he was popular in the ranks, but expected the military to react calmly.
"There will be no military coup," said Pavel Felgengauer, defence analyst for the liberal newspaper Sevodnya.
Yeltsin's demands for reforms have become more shrill since Russia's armed forces were humiliated in a disastrous 21-month campaign against separatist guerrillas in Chechnya.

But many politicians and experts question whether Yeltsin has the determination to push the reforms through. All the signals suggest he is more inclined to cut defence spending than provide the money that could be the ammunition for reform.
The government has targeted defence under plans to reduce overall budget spending, although Rodionov had complained the initial sum was already too little.
"Of course there will be no reform. Yeltsin will take a month or two to find a permanent defence minister and until then he cannot start reforms," Felgengauer said.
"You need economic growth before you can start far-reaching reforms but there is no money for this."

Rodionov's demands for more money probably contributed to his downfall. Yuri Baturin, a Yeltsin defence adviser, has said reforms must be carried out with the money that is available and he fought behind the scenes against Rodionov.
But the problems are not just financial. Reforms can begin only when a military doctrine is worked out and when a decision is taken on what reforms are needed and how much they cost.
"Rodionov should have gone long ago. He was a brake on reforms," said Irina Kobrinskaya of the Moscow office of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
"But Russia's first problem is that it has no military doctrine. It has not even decided where its external threats come from, let alone what reforms it must take and how much they cost."
Despite all Yeltsin's pledges, the state of the armed forces appears to be getting worse.

Some officers and ordinary soldiers have not been paid for months, many are underfed and badly clothed and some have even committed suicide in despair. Corruption is rife and weapons have been stolen from army depots.
Rodionov has issued dire warnings about the state of Russia's nuclear forces and said the army's ability to defend the country is in question.

Alexander Lebed, sacked last October as Yeltsin's security adviser and now one of his main opponents, made clear he expected little good to come of the sackings and that he regarded them as camouflage for Yeltsin's own failings.
"The sackings are a clever way to distract public attention from the complete failure of military reform," Lebed told a news conference.
